claims.text: Arc melting followed by homogenization produces the alloy as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Severe cyclic high-strain-rate loading at cryogenic temperature causes local chemical segregation in the alloy.
Severe mechanical loading causes nanoscale precipitates to develop, especially along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitates act as stress concentrators and potential crack-initiation sites.
The proposed microstructural changes reduce toughness and increase susceptibility to brittle fracture.
Mechanical stresses under the specified extreme conditions drive localized diffusion and segregation.
Localized segregation leads to nucleation of brittle phases at critical microstructural sites.
The resulting brittle phases reduce dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility promotes brittle fracture rather than ductile deformation.
Cryogenically loaded specimens will have lower toughness than the as-homogenized alloy tested under milder conditions.
Cryogenically loaded specimens will exhibit a greater prevalence of brittle-fracture features than the baseline specimens.
Post-test microscopy and compositional analysis will reveal secondary-phase precipitates or grain-boundary segregation in stressed specimens.
No stress-induced microsegregation or phase precipitation is expected under the moderate strain rates and temperatures used for the baseline.
The proposed embrittlement mechanism becomes significant only under high-strain-rate, low-temperature, or high-cycle loading.
At moderate strain rates and room temperature, the alloy retains its toughness without developing precipitate-induced embrittlement.
